title: How Face Blindness Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain prosopagnosia (face blindness), a neurological condition on a spectrum that impairs recognizing faces. They survey the broader family of agnosias (visual, auditory, tactile, such as apperceptive and associative visual agnosia, akinetopsia, phonagnosia, simultanagnosia, autotopagnosia). They cover how normal face perception works (holistic processing, recollection memory tied to faces), coping strategies used by people with the condition (focusing on non-facial cues, using friends, small talk, pretending familiarity, studying important people), the isolation and exhaustion it causes, and famous people reported to have it. They then discuss causes (acquired via brain injury or tumor versus congenital), the first cases studied by Joachim Bodamer in 1944, the fusiform gyrus as the face area, the Cambridge Face Memory Test, the other-race effect in testing, and face recognition in animals. The episode closes with a listener mail about the bombing of California by a Japanese submarine in 1942.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to face blindness
segments.summary: The hosts introduce prosopagnosia as face blindness, a neurological condition existing on a spectrum, and distinguish it from ordinary poor face memory. They share anecdotes about remembering faces and the misconception that people with it see no faces at all.

segments.title: Overview of agnosias
segments.summary: The hosts explain agnosias as recognition impairments, grouped into visual, auditory, and tactile types. They describe apperceptive and associative visual agnosia, akinetopsia, phonagnosia, tactile agnosia, autotopagnosia, and simultanagnosia with examples.

segments.title: How normal face perception works and coping strategies
segments.summary: Face recognition is described as a learned, two-step process: holistic processing of the face, then matching it against memory to retrieve biographical information. People with prosopagnosia rely on non-facial cues like hair, voice, and mannerisms, on friends and family, on small talk, and on studying important people.

segments.title: Living with face blindness: isolation, TV, and famous cases
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the isolation, social anxiety, and exhaustion of the condition, difficulty following TV and movies, and famous people reported to have it, including Oliver Sacks, Jane Goodall, Chuck Close, and Brad Pitt.

segments.title: Causes, history, and diagnosis
segments.summary: Acquired prosopagnosia from brain injury or tumor is contrasted with the more common congenital form. Joachim Bodamer coined the term in 1944 studying German World War Two soldiers with head wounds. Awareness grew slowly; Oliver Sacks wrote about it in 2010. The Cambridge Face Memory Test from 2006 is the main test, which historically used only white male faces, and the other-race effect is raised as a testing concern.

segments.title: Brain basis: fusiform gyrus and evolution
segments.summary: The fusiform gyrus is identified as the main face-recognition area, possibly thicker in congenital cases. A theory from Joe Degutis suggests neural pruning with exposure to faces. Face recognition is discussed as an evolutionary adaptation, and animal face recognition (macaques, sheep, goats) is mentioned.

segments.title: Listener mail: California submarine shelling
segments.summary: A listener named Craig corrects the hosts: a Japanese submarine shelled Ellwood, California, in February 1942, targeting an oil facility.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener emails and sign off.
